title: Optimal decisions and competitor responses (Cournot and Stackelberg)
plain:
This objective puts S21-02 to S21-04 to work. The typical exam steps:

**1. Best response to a given rival output.** Use your reaction function. Rival makes \(Q_2\); you make \(Q_1 = \frac{a - c_1}{2b} - \frac{1}{2}Q_2\).

**2. Cournot equilibrium.** Solve both reaction functions; with identical costs each makes \(\frac{a - c}{3b}\). Price from demand, profit \((P - c)Q\).

**3. Stackelberg.** Leader \(Q_1 = \frac{a + c_2 - 2c_1}{2b}\), follower from its reaction function.

**4. Collusion and cheating.** Joint monopoly: \(Q = \frac{a - c}{2b}\), split evenly. If the rival keeps its quota, your best response is on your reaction function, which is **more** than the quota: cheating pays in a one-shot game (S20 explains when repetition holds it together).

**5. Predicting responses.** A cost cut shifts your reaction function out: you produce more and your rival responds by producing less. A bigger rival output means you produce less.

**The textbook's comparison** of one market, \(P = 1{,}000 - (Q_1 + Q_2)\), \(C_i = 4Q_i\):

| Model | Outputs | Total Q | Price | Profit per firm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Collusion | 249 each | 498 | $502 | $124,002 each |
| Cournot | 332 each | 664 | $336 | $110,224 each |
| Stackelberg (firm 1 leads) | 498 and 249 | 747 | $253 | Leader $124,002, follower $62,001 |
| Bertrand | 498 each | 996 | $4 | $0 |

**Pattern:** output rises and price falls from collusion to Cournot to Stackelberg to Bertrand. The Stackelberg leader earns as much as a colluding firm; the follower earns the least among the quantity models; Bertrand firms earn zero.
why: Practice exam Q31 to Q35 and Comprehension Quiz 10 Q1 to Q3, Q5 and Q6 are expected to be calculations like these.
definition: Optimal decisions in quantity oligopolies come from setting MR = MC given rivals' outputs (Cournot) or given the follower's reaction function (Stackelberg leader); rivals respond along their reaction functions.

formulas.name: Joint monopoly (collusion) output
formulas.note: From MR = a - 2bQ = c; each colluder makes half.

derivation: Unequal costs: substitute \(Q_2 = \frac{a - c_2}{2b} - \frac{Q_1}{2}\) into \(Q_1 = \frac{a - c_1}{2b} - \frac{Q_2}{2}\): \(Q_1 = \frac{a - c_1}{2b} - \frac{a - c_2}{4b} + \frac{Q_1}{4}\), so \(\frac{3}{4}Q_1 = \frac{a - 2c_1 + c_2}{4b}\) and \(Q_1 = \frac{a - 2c_1 + c_2}{3b}\).

math.title: Marginal revenue with two firms
math.body: Revenue for firm 1 is price times its own quantity: \(R_1 = P \cdot Q_1 = [a - b(Q_1 + Q_2)]Q_1 = aQ_1 - bQ_1^2 - bQ_1Q_2\). Take the derivative with respect to \(Q_1\), treating \(Q_2\) as a fixed number: the derivative of \(aQ_1\) is a, of \(bQ_1^2\) is \(2bQ_1\), of \(bQ_1Q_2\) is \(bQ_2\). So \(MR_1 = a - 2bQ_1 - bQ_2\). Tiny example: P = 10 - (Q_1 + Q_2) gives \(MR_1 = 10 - 2Q_1 - Q_2\).

math.title: Solving two reaction functions together
math.body: Substitute one into the other. With \(Q_1 = 5 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q_2\) and \(Q_2 = 5 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q_1\): \(Q_1 = 5 - \tfrac{1}{2}(5 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q_1) = 2.5 + \tfrac{1}{4}Q_1\). Subtract \(\tfrac{1}{4}Q_1\): \(\tfrac{3}{4}Q_1 = 2.5\), so \(Q_1 = 10/3 \approx 3.33\). Then \(Q_2 = 5 - \tfrac{1}{2}(3.33) = 3.33\). With identical firms you can skip the algebra: set \(Q_1 = Q_2 = q\) in one reaction function.

math.title: Profit with constant marginal cost
math.body: With cost \(C = cQ\) and no fixed cost, profit is \((P - c) \times Q\). Example: P = $336, c = $4, Q = 332: profit = 332 × 332 = $110,224.

worked.title: Collusion and cheating
worked.problem: P = 120 - 2(Q_1 + Q_2), MC = $20 for both. (a) Cournot outputs and profit. (b) Collusive outputs and profit. (c) Firm 1's profit if it cheats while firm 2 keeps its quota.
worked.answer: Cheating earns $703.13 > $625, so the cartel is unstable in a one-shot game.

worked.title: Unequal costs
worked.problem: P = 100 - (Q_1 + Q_2), MC_1 = $10, MC_2 = $25. Find the Cournot outputs and price.

graph.caption: The table under the graph compares collusion, Cournot, Stackelberg and Bertrand for the same market. Change the costs to see the responses.

traps: Collusion splits the MONOPOLY output (a - c)/(2b), not the Cournot output.
A cheater's best response comes from its reaction function with the rival at the quota.
Profit is (P - c) × own Q, using the market price from total output.
Lower own cost: produce more; the rival responds by producing less (not more).
